newsitem.title: USA: Miami bond rating is lowest in 43 years.
newsitem.headline: Miami bond rating is lowest in 43 years.

text.p: Miami's financial crisis pushed the city's bond rating to its lowest level since 1953 Friday when Moody's Investors Service reinstated the Baa rating the city first held as it emerged from the Great Depression.

"It's still what is considered by the market to be investment grade," said Moody's rating analyst John Incorvaia. But the rating remains under review by Moody's, and another downgrade would put its bonds in the "junk" category.
Citing Miami's $68 million deficit for the current fiscal year, Moody's cut Miami's general obligation bond rating to Baa from single-A, skipping the intermediate Baa1 rating.
"We know the extent of the problem is great," Incorvaia said. "The fact that they just cut about $30 million from the budget the prior year didn't leave them a whole lot of latitude."

Moody's first rated Miami general obligation bonds in 1938, when it assigned a Ba rating. That was raised to Baa in 1940 as the city moved out of the depression, and then edged up to single-A in 1953.
Miami's Moody rating peaked at A1 in 1969, and then was cut back to single-A in 1992, as the city struggled with suburban flight, refugee influxes and a slowing national economy.
Moody's top rating is Aaa, followed in descending order by Aa1, Aa, A1, A, Baa1 and Baa. Anything below that is considered a junk bond.
Standard & Poor's Corp cut its rating for Miami general obligation bonds to single A from A-plus in 1994, citing the city's continuing use of non-recurring revenues to meet operating expenses.

S&P put the single-A rating on CreditWatch with negative implications on Oct. 4 because of the budget shortfall and was still collecting information about the bail-out plan, said S&P Director Robin Prunty.

"I would imagine within the next week we'll be evaluating that based on the current information that we have," Prunty said. "You're still looking at a city that has vacancies in key administrative posts."

Merrett Stierheim, a former Dade County manager, agreed to act as city manager on an interim basis but plans to step down on Oct. 31. He and a team of corporate volunteers and budget experts on loan from Dade County, are fine-tuning a plan that calls for fee and license increases, service cutbacks, union concessions and the sale of unneeded assets.

"A number of the items, if not all the items, that they (Moody's) critiqued about how the city could get back in the good graces of the rating firms are already under way," said assistant city manager Bill Hampton, one of the volunteers.
The city is also searching for a new city manager to replace Cesar Odio, who resigned last month after he was charged with allegedly accepting kickbacks from city contracts.
Former City Commissioner Miller Dawkins pleaded guilty to two similar counts last week, and prosecutors said former city Finance Director Manohar Surana had agreed to plead guilty to related charges.
The deficit in the $275 million budget for fiscal 1997, which began Oct 1, was not discovered until after Odio and Surana resigned.

Hampton said Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles had agreed to advance the city $22.4 million in sales tax rebates and other state money it otherwise would have received in monthly instalments. The city got the money Friday, he said.
"That doesn't address the inherent long-term problems," Hampton said. "But it helps the city avoid having to go out into the market to borrow money in order to meet operating expenses."
